newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade officials say global telecom pact in sight.
newsitem.headline: Trade officials say global telecom pact in sight.

text.p: Trade officials and negotiators on Thursday signalled growing optimism a global pact opening up world telecommunications markets to competition could be shaped by a deadline set for next February.

Speaking after four days of high-level World Trade Organisation discussions on the elusive deal, they said new offers from the European Union and the United States appeared to have given fresh impetus to the talks.

"I am still not going to stake any money at this stage on getting a deal," the British chairman of the talks, Neil McMillan, told a news briefing. "But the momentum has started to come and I think it's extremely encouraging."
"This is the last chance to have an agreement this century, and it would be foolish to pass it up," McMillan declared.

Karl-Fredrik Falkenberg, chief EU negotiator, said he hoped to see new offers from key developing countries on the table in time for full discussion at the WTO's first conference of trade ministers in Singapore next month.

He told a separate news conference there were only "a few loose ends" to tie up in issues between the two major trading powers and the focus could now switch to the openings to foreign investment and participation offered so far by other countries.

In a statement issued late on Wednesday, U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said the U.S. and EU offers -- tabled jointly this week -- provided a "solid base" for the two to obtain better offers from other partners.

But Lang added: "There is not much time left to conclude these negotiations and significant progress must be made by the Singapore ministerial conference (from December 9-13) if we are to succeed by February."

A deal would put the $600 billion a year global telecommunications market, including satellite services, under rules administered by the WTO and a dispute settlement procedure which means the rules can be enforced.

McMillan, who led earlier WTO negotiations which collapsed in April after the United States baulked at what it saw as poor offers from major emerging economies, said pledges of better packages by December had come in from six countries this week.
These were South Africa, the continent's biggest telecoms market, South Korea, Poland, Mexico, India and Singapore itself. Slovakia, which had stood aloof, had now tabled an offer.

The other two top global trading powers -- Japan and Canada -- had indicated they should be able to come up with new proposals in January, and Brazil, a key Latin American player, had signalled it would also come in then.

"Unfortunately, we have not yet heard anything from Malaysia or Indonesia on their intentions," said McMillan. The United States is especially keen to obtain better access to the telecom markets of the two fast-developing Asian economies.

Falkenberg and McMillan said U.S. officials had removed one problem from the agenda by saying they would settle the issue of the operation of and charging for international phone services in a way that would not violate WTO equal treatment rules.

Washington had been reluctant to open up its own phone market under WTO rules while many countries maintain domestic monopolies that could use their position to charge high prices for incoming calls from the United States.

In another U.S. move clearing a problem with the EU, restrictions were removed from the Washington offer on landing submarine cables on U.S. territory. The EU has pushed forward opening of the major Spanish telecom market from 2003 to 1998.
